newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian banks seen abandoning common lending rates.
newsitem.headline: Indian banks seen abandoning common lending rates.

text.p: India's state-run banks are abandoning the practice of fixing common lending rates with a view to woo clients and boost profitability ahead of plans to raise public funds, analysts said on Thursday.
"I expect different rates emerging from public sector (state-run) banks," K.R. Ramamoorthy, chairman of state-run Corporation Bank, told Reuters by telephone from Bangalore.
The State Bank of India (SBI), India's largest commercial bank, on Thursday announced a one percentage point cut in its prime lending rate to 14.5 percent.

The Bank of Baroda, another state-run bank, announced a half percentage point cut in its lending rate to 15.0 percent on the weekend after the Reserve Bank of India announced steps to boost banks' liquidity and prompt lending rate cuts.
"Banks will now take their own individual decisions," said an executive at another state-run bank.
He said it was significant that the Indian Banks' Association (IBA), a state-run banks management body, did not meet after RBI's weekend monetary policy statement.
State-run banks, which dominate the Indian banking industry, usually take a common approach at IBA meetings, though the association has denied charges of cartelisation.
On Saturday, the RBI said it would cut the mandatory cash reserve ratio (CRR) of banks to 10 percent from 12 percent in four stages, releasing over 85 billion rupees into bank coffers.

RBI said the one percentage point cut would be implemented by November 9, but an additional cut of one percentage point in January would be "contingent on the monetary and price situation at that time".
Many banking analysts had expected SBI to cut lending rates by half a percentage point, as Bank of Baroda did.
"I thought what Bank of Baroda did was logical as the second one percentage cut in CRR is conditional," said Sandeep Nanda, head of research at NatWest Securities in Bombay.
Corporation Bank's Ramamoorthy said he did not expect clients to switch banks because of the divergent rates.
Some company treasurers agreed. "Large corporates won't shift because of half or one percentage cuts," said Anil Singhvi, treasure at Gujarat Ambuja Cements.
"Banks now realise they have their own problems -- capital adequacy, non-performing assets and the like -- and can't have common lending rates," said Prabodh Agarwal, analyst at James Capel B&K.
"Banks like SBI have low-cost funds and high non-fund based incomes -- they have 40 percent of India's foreign exchange business. SBI can afford to charge lower rates," Agarwal said.

Some analysts said the divergent lending rates also reflect increasing accountability of state-run bank managements ahead of plans to divest government holdings through initial public offerings planned later this year.
